x+\pi & \text { for } & x \in[-\pi, 0) \\
\pi \cos x & \text { for } & x \in\left[0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right] \\
\left(x-\frac{\pi}{2}\right)^2 & \text { for } & x \in\left(\frac{\pi}{2}, \pi\right]
\end{array}\right.$
Consider the following statements:

For differentiability,
L.H.D. = R.H.D.
Thus at $x=0\begin{aligned} \text { L.H.D. } & =\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(0-h)-f(0)}{-h} \\ & =\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(-h)-f(0)}{-h} \\ & =\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{(-h+\pi)-(\pi \cos 0)}{-h}=1 \\ \text { L.H.D. }= & 1 \\ \text { R.H.D. } & =\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(0+h)-f(0)}{h} \\ & =\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(h)-f(0)}{h} \\ & =\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{\pi \cos h-\pi \cos 0}{h} \\ & =\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{\pi[\cos h-1]}{h}\end{aligned}\begin{aligned} & =\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{\pi\left[1-\frac{h^2}{2!}+\frac{h^4}{4!} \ldots \ldots-1\right]}{h} \\ & =\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{\pi\left[1-\frac{1}{2} h^2+\frac{1}{24} h^4 \ldots . .-1\right]}{h} \\ & =\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{\pi\left[-\frac{1}{2} h^2+\frac{1}{24} h^4 \ldots \ldots\right]}{h}=0\end{aligned}\text { L.H.D. } \neq \text { R.H.D. }$

questions.q:
A function $\mathrm{f}(\mathrm{x})$ is defined as follows:
$f(x)=\left\{\begin{array}{ccc}
x+\pi & \text { for } & x \in[-\pi, 0) \\
\pi \cos x & \text { for } & x \in\left[0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right] \\
\left(x-\frac{\pi}{2}\right)^2 & \text { for } & x \in\left(\frac{\pi}{2}, \pi\right]
\end{array}\right.$
Consider the following statements:
1. The function $\mathrm{f}(\mathrm{x})$ is continuous at $\mathrm{x}=0$.
2. The function $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=\frac{\pi}{2}$.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.solution:
Given
$f(x)=\left\{\begin{array}{cc}
(x+\pi) & \text { for } x \in[-\pi, 0) \\
\pi \cos x & \text { for } x \in\left[0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right] \\
\left(x-\frac{\pi}{2}\right)^2 & \text { for } x \in\left(\frac{\pi}{2}, \pi\right]
\end{array}\right.$
For continuity,
$\begin{aligned}
& f(a)=\text { L.H.L. }=\text { R.H.L. } \\
& \begin{aligned}
& \text { At } x=0 \\
& f(0)=\pi \cos 0=\pi \\
& \text { L.H.L. }=\lim _{x \rightarrow 0^{-}} f(x-h) \\
&=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} f(-h) \\
&=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0}(-h+\pi)=\pi
\end{aligned}
\end{aligned}\begin{aligned}
\text { R.H.L. } & =\lim _{x \rightarrow 0^{+}} f(x+h) \\
& =\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} f(0+h) \\
& =\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \pi \cos h \\
& =\pi \cos 0=\pi
\end{aligned}f(0)=\text { L.H.L. }=\text { R.H.L. }$
Hence function is continuous at $x=0$. 
Statement (1) is correct.
At $x=\frac{\pi}{2}\begin{aligned}
\text { L.H.L. } & =\lim _{x \rightarrow \frac{\pi^{-}}{2}} f(x-h) \\
& =\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} f\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-h\right) \\
& =\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \pi \cos \left(\frac{\pi}{2}-h\right) \\
& =\pi \cos \frac{\pi}{2}=0
\end{aligned}\begin{aligned}
\text { RH.L. } & =\lim _{x \rightarrow \frac{\pi^{+}}{2}} f(x+h) \\
& =\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} f\left(\frac{\pi}{2}+h\right) \\
& =\lim _{h \rightarrow 0}\left(\frac{\pi}{2}+h-\frac{\pi}{2}\right)^2=0
\end{aligned}\begin{aligned}
& f\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)=\pi \cos \frac{\pi}{2}=0 \\
& \text { L.H.L. }=\text { R.H.L. }=f\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)
\end{aligned}$
Hence function is continuous at $x=\frac{\pi}{2}$
Statement (2) is correct.

$\begin{aligned} f(x) & =\frac{27}{4}\left(x^{2 / 3}-x\right) \\ & =\frac{27}{4}\left(\left(x^2\right)^{1 / 3}-x\right)\end{aligned}$ For $f(x)=1\begin{aligned} & \frac{27}{4}\left(\left(x^2\right)^{1 / 3}-x\right)=1 \\ & \left(x^{1 / 3}\right)^2-x=\frac{4}{27} \end{aligned}$ Put $x^{1 / 3}=yx=y^3\begin{aligned} & y^2-y^3=\frac{4}{27} \\ & \Rightarrow y^3-y^2+\frac{4}{27}=0 \\ & \Rightarrow 27 y^3-27 y^2+4=0 \end{aligned}$ This is a cubic equation. If we put $y=-\frac{1}{3}$ then $(3 y+1)=0$ is a factor of cubic equation.
$\begin{aligned} & (3 y+1)\left(9 y^2-12 y+4\right)=0 \\ & (3 y+1)(3 y-2)^2=0 \end{aligned}$ Hence $y=-\frac{1}{3}, \frac{2}{3}$ Thus $f(x)=1$ has two solutions.

$\begin{aligned}
& A=\left[\begin{array}{cc}
-1 & 1 \\
1 & -1
\end{array}\right] \\
& A \cdot A=\left[\begin{array}{cc}
-1 & 1 \\
1 & -1
\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{cc}
-1 & 1 \\
1 & -1
\end{array}\right] \\
& =\left[\begin{array}{cc}
2 & -2 \\
-2 & 2
\end{array}\right]=-2\left[\begin{array}{cc}
-1 & 1 \\
1 & -1
\end{array}\right] \\
& A^2=-2 A \\
& A^2 \cdot A=-2\left[\begin{array}{cc}
-1 & 1 \\
1 & -1

-2 & 2
\end{array}\right]=4\left[\begin{array}{cc}

& A^3=4 A
\end{aligned}$

& \Rightarrow \log x=\log z \Rightarrow x=z

& \Rightarrow x=y=z \\
& x \cdot y \cdot z=64 \\
& x=y=z=4
\end{aligned}$
Thus $x, y, z$ are in A.P. and G.P. both.

questions.q: The mean of the series $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ is $\overline{\mathrm{X}}$. If $\mathrm{x}_2$ is replaced by $\lambda$, then what is the new mean?
questions.solution:
Mean of series $\left(x_1, x_2, x_3 \ldots \ldots x_{\mathrm{n}}\right)\begin{aligned}
& \bar{x}=\frac{x_1+x_2+x_3+\ldots . x_n}{n} \\
& \Rightarrow x_1+x_2+x_3+\ldots . x_n=n \bar{x}
\end{aligned}$
Now we will replace $x_2$ by $\lambda$ so no. of elements in series will not change.
New series will include $\lambda$ and exclude $x_2$
Hence new series sum :
$\left(x_1+x_2+\ldots . . x_n\right)-x_2+\lambda=n \bar{x}+\lambda-x_2$
Now new mean $=\frac{n \bar{x}+\lambda-x_2}{n}=\frac{n \bar{x}-x_2+\lambda}{n}$

questions.q:
Consider the function $\mathrm{f}(\theta)=4\left(\sin ^2 \theta+\cos ^4 \theta\right)$
What is the minimum value of the function $f(\theta)$ ?
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned} f(\theta)= & 4\left(\sin ^2 \theta+\cos ^4 \theta\right) \\ = & 4\left(\sin ^2 \theta+\cos ^2 \theta\left(1-\sin ^2 \theta\right)\right) \\ = & 4\left(\sin ^2 \theta+\cos ^2 \theta-\sin ^2 \theta \cos ^2 \theta\right) \\ = & 4\left(1-\frac{1}{4} \sin ^2 2 \theta\right) \\ & {[\because \sin 2 \theta=2 \sin \theta \cos \theta] }\end{aligned}$
For minimum value of $f(\theta), \sin ^2 2 \theta$ should be maximum i.e. $\sin ^2 2 \theta=1$.
$\left.f(\theta)\right|_{\min }=4\left(1-\frac{1}{4}(1)\right)=4 \times \frac{3}{4}=3$

Consider the function $f(\theta)=4\left(\sin ^2 \theta+\cos ^4 \theta\right)$
Consider the following statements:

2. $\mathrm{f}(\theta)=\frac{7}{2}$ has a solution.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned} f(\theta)= & 4\left(\sin ^2 \theta+\cos ^4 \theta\right) \\ = & 4\left(\sin ^2 \theta+\cos ^2 \theta\left(1-\sin ^2 \theta\right)\right) \\ = & 4\left(\sin ^2 \theta+\cos ^2 \theta-\sin ^2 \theta \cos ^2 \theta\right) \\ = & 4\left(1-\frac{1}{4} \sin ^2 2 \theta\right) \\ & {[\because \sin 2 \theta=2 \sin \theta \cos \theta] }\end{aligned}\begin{aligned}

& \Rightarrow \sin ^2 2 \theta=2 \\
& \Rightarrow \sin 2 \theta= \pm \sqrt{2}
\end{aligned}$
Since $\sin \theta$ cannot have vlaue greater than $1\&$ less than -1.
Hence $f(\theta)=2$ has no solution.
$\begin{aligned} & f(\theta)=\frac{7}{2} \\ & 4\left(1-\frac{1}{4} \sin ^2 2 \theta\right)=\frac{7}{2} \\ & \Rightarrow\left(1-\frac{1}{4} \sin ^2 2 \theta\right)=\frac{7}{8}\end{aligned}\begin{aligned}
& \Rightarrow-\frac{1}{4} \sin ^2 2 \theta=\frac{7}{8}-1 \\

& \Rightarrow \sin ^2 2 \theta=\frac{1}{2} \\

& \Rightarrow \sin 2 \theta=\sin ( \pm \pi / 4) \\
& \Rightarrow 2 \theta= \pm \pi / 4 \\
& \theta=( \pm) \frac{\pi}{8}
\end{aligned}$
Hence $f(\theta)=\frac{7}{2}$ has a solution.

What is the value of $\sin \frac{\mathrm{A}}{2} \sin \frac{B}{2} \sin \frac{C}{2}$ ?
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \text { Given } \cos A+\cos B+\cos C=\sqrt{3} \sin \frac{\pi}{3} \\ & \cos A+\cos B+\cos C \\ & =2 \cos \frac{A+B}{2} \cdot \cos \frac{A-B}{2}+\left(1-2 \sin ^2 \frac{C}{2}\right)  \\ & =2 \sin \frac{C}{2} \cos \frac{A-B}{2}+1-2 \sin ^2 \frac{C}{2} \left(\because \frac{A+B}{2}=90^{\circ}-\frac{C}{2}\right)\\ & =1+2 \sin \frac{C}{2}\left[\cos \frac{A-B}{2}-\sin \frac{C}{2}\right] \\ & =1+2 \sin \frac{C}{2}\left[\cos \frac{A-B}{2}-\cos \frac{A+B}{2}\right] \\ & =1+4 \sin \frac{C}{2} \sin \frac{A}{2} \sin \frac{B}{2} \\ & \cos A+\cos B+\cos C=\sqrt{3} \sin \frac{\pi}{3} \\ & 1+4 \sin \frac{C}{2} \sin \frac{A}{2} \sin \frac{B}{2}=\sqrt{3} \sin \frac{\pi}{3}\end{aligned}\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow 1+4 \sin \frac{C}{2} \sin \frac{A}{2} \sin \frac{B}{2}=\sqrt{3} \times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ & \Rightarrow 4 \sin \frac{A}{2} \sin \frac{B}{2} \sin \frac{C}{2}=\frac{3}{2}-1\end{aligned}\sin \frac{A}{2} \sin \frac{B}{2} \sin \frac{C}{2}=\frac{1}{8}$
